delves.blurb: Behind a rusted door on the fifth floor, something is still going clank, clank, clank. Nobody has worked the pumps in years. So who's working them now?

a.say:
A side tunnel ends at an iron door stencilled PUMP ROOM 1. From behind it comes a slow, patient sound: clank... clank... clank.

The mine was sealed for years. Something in there has been working all on its own the whole time.

knock.say:
You knock. The clanking stops.

There is a long, thoughtful pause. Then, very politely, it starts again: clank... clank.

room.say:
Inside, a great iron beam see-saws over a pit, driven by a little waterwheel in an underground stream. Each stroke works a pump rod that squeals like a gull.

One of the pins holding the beam has worked nearly loose. Every stroke it slips a little further. A few hundred more, and the whole thing comes down.

slip.say:
You swing, miss the pin and hit the beam, which rings like a dinner gong. Every bat on the fifth floor has something to say about it.

The pin slides out another inch.

mira.say:
Clevis pin's walked. Grandad built these to run a hundred years if somebody greased them now and then. Nobody did.

Hold the lamp. One tap. Two, if you breathe on me.

fixed.say:
The pin seats home with a clunk, and the pump settles into a smooth, easy rhythm: whoosh... whoosh. The squealing stops.

On a shelf by the door, under a thick fur of dust, sits the pumpman's tin. Inside: a pencil stub, a lemon drop gone to glass, and a note.

note.say:
GONE UP FOR THE FLOOD MEETING. BACK BY SIX. SHE'LL KEEP GOING ON HER OWN. GREASE HER TUESDAYS. NED.

Ned never came back down; the mine was sealed that night. And the pump kept going on her own, just as he said, keeping the top floors dry all these years with nobody to grease her.

ch.t: Grease the rod with candle wax
Pat the pump and say well done

win.say:
You leave the door propped open so the pump can hear the rest of the mine. Whoosh... whoosh. She sounds pleased with herself.

Just outside you find Ned's ore barrow, still half full from his last shift. It seems a shame to waste it.

lose.say:
This feels like a job for someone with more tools and fewer bats. You back out, and the clanking follows you all the way to the stairs, patient as ever.

It's waited years. It can wait a little longer.

delves.blurb: A doorway carved with ivy leaves opens on a little chapel the miners built underground. Half the roof has come down. The other half is waiting to see what you'll do.

a.say:
A doorway carved with ivy leaves opens on a chapel cut from the living rock: three stone benches, a shelf for candles, and a round window carved in the wall where no daylight has ever come.

The back of the roof has fallen in a long slope of rubble. Something under it catches your lamp and glints.

ch.t: Light a candle on the shelf

lit.say:
One candle, and the whole chapel glows. The walls are carved all over: names, dates, little pictures. A pick. A loaf. A cat. A baby in a basket.

And over and over, in a dozen different hands: HOME BY SIX. Like a wish. Like a promise.

oakley.say:
The Miners' Chapel! It's in the minutes of eighteen eighty-seven! They held a harvest supper down here, with a brass band. The band did not enjoy it.

The minutes say the roof rests on a king post. Just there, behind the rubble. If we shore that up first... oh, how splendid. I'm being useful.

rubble.say: The rubble is loose, and the roof above it looks... thoughtful. Poking out from under the stones is the corner of a small wooden box.

ch.t: Dig it out, stone by stone
Prop the roof with planks first

rumble.say:
One stone slides. Then three. Then the roof makes a deep, grumbling noise, and dust pours down like flour through a sieve.

You freeze. The chapel holds its breath with you.

box.say:
The box comes free. Inside, wrapped in a scrap of blue flannel, is a brass pocket lantern no bigger than an egg, and a card in looping, old-fashioned writing:

FOR WHOEVER COMES NEXT. KEEP IT LIT. HOME BY SIX.

win.say:
The little lantern catches at once and burns small and steady, as if it's only been waiting to be asked.

By the door stands the chapel's ore box, where every miner left a lump from each shift for the harvest supper. Nobody has emptied it in years. You take it up, along with the lantern, and head home. It's nearly six.

lose.say:
You back out of the chapel one careful step at a time. Behind you the roof settles with a long, grumbling sigh, and then goes quiet.

The box will keep. Whatever's in it has waited this long.

delves.blurb: On the fifteenth floor, the way to the next good seam runs straight through a cavern with an enormous cave bear asleep in it. Tread lightly.

a.say:
The tunnel opens into a cavern, warm and close and smelling of old hay. Filling most of it, rising and falling like a breathing hill, is a bear.

A cave bear: huge, shaggy, snoring a snore you can feel through your boots. The tunnel you need is on the far side of it.

tobin.say:
Bear's dreaming. Fish, I'd say. Look at the paws go.

Step when it snores. Stop when it don't. Same as wading past a heron.

crunch.say:
Your boot finds the one dry bone on the whole cavern floor. CRUNCH.

The snoring stops. One great eye opens, gold as a lamp, and regards you for a long, long moment.

ch.t: Back away the way you came

paw.say:
The bear sleeps on. Close up, you can see why it sleeps so badly: a long splinter of old pit-prop is wedged between two of its toes, and the pad around it is red and sore.

It whimpers in its sleep, like a dog dreaming of baths.

ch.t: Tiptoe on and let it sleep

stir.say:
The splinter's in deep. The bear grumbles in its sleep and tucks the paw under its chin, out of reach.

After a minute it pushes the paw back out again, as if it's thought better of it.

ch.t: Tiptoe on and let it sleep

eased.say:
The splinter slides free. The bear lets out a vast, warm sigh that ruffles your hair and curls up tighter, and its snore changes: softer, slower, almost a purr.

You'd swear it's smiling.

win.say:
Past the bear, the tunnel climbs to a ledge and a fat seam of silver. On the ledge, someone has left a smooth grey stone and a note.

FOR THE NEXT ONE SCARED OF THE BEAR. I WAS TOO. RUB THE STONE. IT HELPS. RUTH, SHIFT BOSS.

You rub it. It helps.

lose.say:
The bear huffs, rolls over and flops right across the tunnel mouth. Well. That decides that.

You back out one slow step at a time, until the snoring is just a rumble in the rock behind you. Another day, another way round.

delves.blurb: A cavern of sky crystal where every sound comes back sweeter. The old miners called it the Choir. Its far door won't open for anyone who can't carry a tune.

a.say:
The tunnel opens into a cavern lined with sky crystal, thousands of pale blue points catching your lamp. You say “oh” without meaning to, and the cavern says it back, softer each time, until the last is barely a breath.

A crack runs across the floor, too wide to step. Beyond it stands a round door of solid crystal.

slide.say:
Your boot skids, and you sit down hard on a crystal, which rings like a struck glass. The whole cavern rings with it, a great shivering chord, and fine blue dust drifts down.

Ow, says the Choir, a hundred times over.

door.say:
The crystal door has no handle and no keyhole. Carved above it, in miners' capitals: SING HER HOME.

When you hum, the door shivers. When you hum higher, it goes still. It's listening for one note in particular.

ch.t: Tap the walls to find the note

sour.say:
You hum. The door hums back, sourly, like a cat stroked the wrong way. The crystals all around buzz, and somewhere a small one cracks.

There are scratches on the door you can't quite make out by lamplight. Lines. Maybe writing.

ch.t: Light a candle and look closer

notes.say:
In the candlelight, the scratches turn into music: five lines, a handful of notes, and underneath, very small: iron from the sky, ring the valley home.

The old skipping song. Every child in Bramblebrook knows it. Of course.

pip.say:
It's humming the skipping song! Can't you hear it? Dum, dum, de-dum!

Iron from the sky, ring the valley HOME! Did it work? It's working! Sir Hopsalot, it's WORKING!

win.say:
The note goes into the door, and the door gives it back fuller, deeper, sweeter: the low, round note of a great bell. The crystals take it up until the whole cavern is ringing.

The door swings open on a small chamber glittering with gold, where the miners stacked the Choir's best finds and, it seems, forgot to come back for them.

lose.say:
You back out of the Choir on tiptoe. The crystals hum a little after you've gone, then fall quiet, waiting.

They'll still be listening whenever you come back with the right song.

delves.blurb: The floodwater from Gallery Six had to go somewhere. It went down. Someone went down after it the night of the flood, and left something behind.

a.say:
The floodwater from Gallery Six had to go somewhere. On the twenty-fifth floor you find where it went: a long, low gallery half full of still black water, a rail track running into it, and a stencil on the wall.

GALLERY 6, LOWER. DEEP WORKINGS. MIND THE SLUICE.

ch.t: Hang a lantern on the old hook

lit.say:
The lantern swings on its hook and the gallery wakes up: glowcaps in every crack, old timbers, and a narrow stone ledge along the wall just above the waterline that you'd never have seen in the dark.

Someone chalked arrows along it, long ago. They all point the same way.

dunk.say:
The rails end. You don't, quite. There's a cold, polite gulp, and you're in up to your neck, spluttering, lamp held high.

Your feet find the rails again a few steps on. Wetter, colder, but still going.

sluice.say:
At the far end, a great iron sluice gate holds back the rest of the water, with a wheel beside it, rusted solid.

Chalked on the gate, faded but clear: A.A. WAS HERE. LAMP OUT, WATER RISING. GONE UP. WREN'S TROWEL ON THE SHELF. TELL HER SORRY.

The shelf is behind the gate.

ch.t: Let Mira see to the sluice

jam.say:
The wheel turns a quarter inch and stops dead with a groan that echoes all the way down the gallery. Rust drifts down like red snow.

It needs more leverage than two arms can give it.

mira.say:
A.A. That's Abel. Grandad's brother. Family story says he got out the night of the flood and never came down again. Now I know where he was.

Right. Ratchet's seized, but there's a pawl you knock up first. Grandad always hid them. Like so.

drained.say:
The gate lifts. The water slides away with a long, satisfied gurgle, and the gallery floor appears: rails, a toppled barrow, gold glittering in the silt.

On a high, dry shelf, right where the chalk said, lies a gardener's trowel. A worn ash handle with W.B. burned into the wood.

win.say:
Under the trowel, folded small, is a note in shaky pencil:

Borrowed this to dig for Wren's humming rock. Lamp went out in the flood and I ran for it. Sorry, Wren. Deeper still, I reckon. Abel.

The trowel fits your hand as if it's been waiting for it. You fill your pack from the silt and start the long climb up.

lose.say:
You climb back to the stairs, dripping, and the gallery settles into its black stillness behind you.

Whatever's on that shelf has stayed dry all these years. It can stay dry a little longer.

delves.blurb: Past the deepest of the old workings, a round chamber hums one low, sweet note. This is where the rest of the bell's star came to rest.

a.say:
Past the deepest of the old workings, the tunnel turns smooth. Glassy. As if something very hot came through here very fast, a very long time ago.

It ends in a round chamber shaped like the inside of a bell. In the middle, half sunk in the floor, sits a lump of dark iron the size of a hay cart. It's humming.

walls.say:
By the entrance lie two old picks, rusted to lace, side by side. Someone got this far once, long ago, heard the hum and decided it was none of their business.

Scratched into the glassy wall beside them: SHE'S STILL WARM. LEFT HER BE.

star.say:
Up close, the star-iron is warm. Not hot: warm, like a loaf an hour out of the oven. The hum goes through your hand, up your arm, and settles somewhere behind your ribs.

It's the bell's note. The very same. You'd know it anywhere.

glow.say:
The glowcaps pulse in time with the hum: bright, dim, bright. All round the star-iron they shine, except on one side, where they barely glow at all.

There. That's where the hum runs lowest. That's where it will give.

ring.say:
Your pick strikes, and the whole vault RINGS: one enormous note that shakes dust from the ceiling and rattles every tooth in your head.

Far above, you're fairly sure, Tobin's line goes slack and Hazel's cat sits bolt upright.

ch.t: Leave before the roof joins in

wren.say:
Eight winters on a mountain working out where here was. And here it is. Hello, you.

Don't hit it; it'll only sulk. Listen for the flat spot, where it hums lowest. There. Tap it kindly and it'll give you a piece as a present.

shard.say:
A sliver of star-iron comes away in your hand, dark and warm, with a silver shimmer where the lamp catches it. Then a second drops beside it, as if the star has decided you can have two.

The hum doesn't fade. If anything, it sounds pleased.

win.say:
It's a long climb with star-iron in your pack and the hum still in your bones. Far above, the Bramble Bell hangs over the square, cast from another piece of this very same star.

They've been apart a long, long time. Tonight they're a little less apart.

lose.say:
You back out of the vault, and the hum follows you up the tunnel, patient and unbothered.

It's been waiting since before there was a valley. Another day won't hurt it.

delves.blurb: Below the star-iron vault, a stair winds down to a still black lake that reflects a sky full of stars. There is half a mile of rock overhead.

a.say:
Below the vault, a stair no miner cut winds down and down until your lamp finds water: a lake, black and perfectly still. In it, reflected, is the night sky. Stars, hundreds of them. There's half a mile of rock over your head.

A little boat is tied to an iron ring at your feet, half full of water. Far out across the lake, something glints.

ch.t: Bail the boat and patch it

sink.say:
Your patch holds for six strokes. On the seventh, a jet of icy water hits you in the face, and the stars in the lake go wobbly.

You row back to shore a good deal faster than you rowed out, sitting in a puddle.

ch.t: Leave the lake to its stars

tobin.say:
Boat's sound. Just thirsty. Wood swells, leak stops. Give her a minute.

...

There. Ferried forty years. Never a lake with stars in. Sit still. Don't trail your hand.

ch.t: Sit still and let him row

row.say:
The boat slides out over the stars. Each stroke breaks them into silver ripples, and they settle again behind you. It's very quiet, the kind of quiet you could lean on.

The glint becomes an island: a flat rock, a stone hut no taller than you, and a brass telescope on a stand, pointing straight down into the water.

island.say:
Beside the telescope is a slate: OBSERVATIONS FROM BELOW. Under it run columns of figures in a careful, tiny hand, three hundred years old.

Someone stood here, long ago, and charted the sky by looking down.

scope.say:
Through the telescope the reflected sky leaps close: the Bell Star, low and steady, right where Rook always says. And beneath it, small and clear in the water, a pinprick of warm light.

Rook's lighthouse. You're looking at the valley's own sky, from underneath.

ch.t: Go and look in the hut

wren.say:
Good heavens. These are the observatory's numbers. Before there was an observatory.

Someone tracked the star that fell, followed it all the way down here, and kept watching the sky from underneath. Of course they did. It's what I'd have done, with better knees.

ch.t: Go and look in the hut

win.say:
Inside the hut, wrapped in oilcloth, is a wooden box of stones from the lake bed, gems and star-iron jumbled together, each glowing faintly. On top, a note: FOR THE NEXT STARGAZER. I SUPPOSE THAT'S YOU.

You row back over the stars with the box on your knees and don't say a word the whole way. It doesn't seem the place.

lose.say:
You tie the boat back to its ring and climb the long stair, the stars in the water carrying on without you.

They'll still be there. Down here, nothing much changes, and nothing is in a hurry.

delves.blurb: Forty floors down, past the vault and the lake, there's a light under a door. And, impossibly, the smell of tea.

a.say:
Forty floors down, the tunnel narrows to a crack, then opens over a chasm so deep your lamp can't find the bottom. Across it: a ledge, a round oak door, and a line of warm yellow light underneath.

Also, faintly, impossibly: the smell of tea.

balk.say:
You run, you jump, and at the very last moment your legs have a quick word with each other and decide against it. You stop at the edge, windmilling, and sit down hard.

A pebble goes over. You never hear it land.

ch.t: Go home and think about it

door.say:
The door has no handle, only a ring of seven brass dials, each stamped with a little picture: a wheat ear, a fish, a leaf, a pick, a hammer, a spoon and a bell.

Above them, in old letters: WHAT MENDS A VALLEY?

ch.t: Turn every dial, one by one
Let Mira listen to the dials

jam.say:
Click. Whirr. Every dial spins back to the start, and the door gives a small, offended clunk.

From behind it, faintly, a kettle begins to sing. Whatever the answer is, somebody in there is very relaxed about it.

ch.t: Ease the dials with candle wax
Leave the door to its secrets

mira.say:
Seven tumblers. It doesn't want one answer, it wants all of them. Farming, fishing, the lot. Whoever built this had a sense of humour.

Hold the lamp. And don't breathe on my dials.

room.say:
Click, click, click, and the door swings open on a small round room, warm as a kitchen. In the grate, a lump of star-iron glows like embers, and on it a copper kettle sings. Two armchairs, a shelf of cups, and on the table a fat leather book.

The book is a guestbook. The first entry is three hundred years old.

book.say:
Names, in a dozen hands, one every few decades: miners, a stonemason, an astronomer with very small writing. Each left a line. Kettle was on. Kettle on again! STILL ON. Who IS doing this?

Nobody ever found out. You check the kettle. It's on.

ch.t: Sign your name and pour a cup

wren.say:
Oh, I'm going in this book. Stand back.

W. Bramble, gardener. Late, as usual. Tea excellent. There.

Your turn. Then we drink this and never tell Clementine. She'd want to bake down here.

ch.t: Sign your name and pour a cup

win.say:
You write {name} under the last entry, and a line of your own. Then you sit by the star-iron fire with a cup of tea that tastes faintly of honey and thunderstorms.

Under the table is a chest, and on it a card: FOR THE ROAD BACK UP. TAKE WHAT YOU NEED. LEAVE THE KETTLE ON.

You do both.

lose.say:
You head back up the long dark way. The smell of tea follows you for three whole floors before it gives up.

Whoever keeps that kettle on will keep it on. There's always another day for tea.
